en: His shout was fire,
His figure vast beyond measure.
Gray-maned Manas, the leopard,
Joined those three
As their companion, that magnanimous lion,
And himself pursued the foe.
“Drive them, children, drive!” he cried,
“Seize the monster’s son!
He will not heed my pleas—
Strike your spears into his waist!
Wage true war,
Cut him down and finish him!
Stand face-to-face,
Raise the battle cry of ‘Manas!’
And unleash a dreadful battle!
Drive them, children, drive!” he cried,
And noble Manas, the beloved lion,
Himself shouted encouragement.
They seemed an army beyond counting;
Your heroic father, brave Manas,
Joined the three tempestuous warriors
As their companion.
Behind them the beloved lion
Appeared in human form,
And the mind of anyone who looked closely
Reeled in astonishment.
From the edge of the northern quarter came one
Who spared no life in battle
And never drank his fill of blood;
Who broke through dead ends and opened roads,
And when countless enemies came,
Charged straight into their midst;
Who never recoiled from glowing embers
Nor flinched and fled from flame;
A master horseman, watchful on the road—
Syrgak, warrior of the magnanimous lion,
Who never drew back once he thrust,
Never lost the trail of the dejected,
And in darkness never mistook
Or missed a shadow’s track.
Broad-bodied and short in stature,
His whole frame was black stone;
Thick-armed and stone-hearted,
A sturdy, well-built giant.
He raised his socketed spear
High above him,
And from hosts that closed in combat
He never stirred or retreated.
Whoever came within his reach,
He crushed into the earth like a sheep.
When black muskets cracked
And fierce matchlocks snapped,
He never started or drew back.
Before enemies pouring upon him,
He never retreated in fear.
He faced giants and ogres,
And none he fought escaped alive.
Breaking away with some forty warriors,
Brave Syrgak of Khan Ulak
Appeared, stunning the mind,
As though alive;
He shouted, “Hero!”
And called out for Külchoro.
No soul could withstand his wrath;
Genial Syrgak, the lion hero,
Again leveled his spear.
To the three in that battle,
He gave his aid as a comrade.
If you looked to this side,
There rode one upon Aisarala.
Though foes were tens of thousands,
He swept them away in every battle.
He wore yellow rawhide trousers,
Bore a spear without a tassel,
And girded a sword without a sheath,
Biting hard upon his lip.
He wound his sash around his waist
And cast the world into tumult.
Tall and broad-shouldered,
Both wrestler and lion,
From the city of the Khakhan
Came this fierce lion from China.
The mighty hero gave a shout;
The earth broke and heaved,
As though seven thousand troops had come.
Straining like a lion,
He readied and leveled his spear,
Shouting from the front,
Calling to the hero Külchoro,
His only son.
Power rang from his battle cry,
And from the fire on either side
Hair enough for socks was singed away.
The hero Külchoro
Was accompanied by your uncle.
Raging and charging,
He prepared to face the foe.
“My broad-shouldered uncle Külchoro,
You are a spring flowing down the valley,
A lamp seen among the people.
You are a legacy left by a hero,
A noble one remaining as his sign.
The fierce enemy Sarybay
Has battled you beyond capture;
Alas, how fares my son?” he cried.
Taking a shortcut along the narrow path,
From before his khanly nephew,
He led Buurul, the horse ridden to battle,
Urging it hurriedly onward,
And shouted encouragement.
The mighty hero whose patron spirit lived,
The lord supported by the holy spirits,
Himself accompanied him.
The Sarala beneath him
Shone as though touched by moonlight;
A red banner with a golden crescent
Fluttered in his hand.
“Charge, my son, charge!” he cried,
“Hold your spear ready!
Let me see what troubles you.
Against Sarybay, whom you must fight,
Clashing and thrusting,
I shall stand beside you.
Let me see the measure
Of that swine Sarybay!
You were a hero, you were a lion,
A warrior who knew the enemy’s ways.
Level your spear and break their ranks;
In fury, drive the enemy away!
Your heroic father is beside you—
Now unleash true slaughter!
Sarybay, who has challenged us,
Has shown his enmity thus.
Do not spare your precious life,
Do not glance to either side.
Level your spear and thrust it home,
Drive your spear in till it drips with blood,
Pierce both his eyes!
That swaggering brute,
That thick-armed would-be wrestler,
Has raised this great commotion from the start.
Rip open his belly like a donkey’s!
Choose your opening and thrust without wavering,
Drive it home before he can flinch,
Twist the spear in openly,
Watch him closely and strike!
Tear the flesh from the shins
Of that raging swine.
Keep clear of the crush and thrust,
Face him without fear and thrust!
Let dust rise where your spear strikes,
Let blood gush where your fist falls,
Let life flow mingled with the blood!
Let the true spear reach its mark,
And let not a scrap of the swine remain—
Let them all be ground to dust!
Thrust with unblinking eyes,
Gather all your wisdom and strength,
And at that gaudy swine
Strike swiftly till he topples.
Aim carefully and thrust,
Aim for the place that brings death.
Choose his flank and thrust;
Strike surely, not as he does.
Let me see the grievous wrath
Of that swaggering swine.
You have fought many times
Against that strong-armed swine;
My heroic son Külchoro,
Let me stand as your support.
Do not look around you;
This world is vain and deceitful—
Spare not your life at all!
Do not consider what is precious;
Spare not even your threadlike life!
Charge, my son, charge!” he cried,
“Give that fearsome swine
No chance to flee—finish him!
No man escapes his destined death,
No one turns back from dying.
Unleash a fierce battle,
Until not a hair’s breadth remains whole,
And slaughter one another.
Such is the harshness of battle.
Charge, my son, charge!” he cried,
“Seize that swine
Whom the whole world could not overcome!
Beat out his fury in earnest
And settle the final reckoning!
Grapple and wrench each other,
And test yourselves in combat.
Single out the forces
In which the swine places his trust;
Learn the measure of their courage,
And slice their bellies like fat.
Turn the river from its course,
And until you die in battle,
Slaughter the swine who came himself
As though fire had swept over him.
Smash him into dust,
Bathe the sword in blood,
And strike down all around him.
Beat out completely the rage
Of the wrathful boar—
Such is the nature of battle.
Let me see his prowess;
I came seeking you,
To grapple with him and spill his blood.”
His voice was heard, though he was unseen.
When he heard this news,
Choro, son of Almambet, said,
“That is my father’s voice,”
His heart filled with burning grief.
In the blink of an eye,
This wretched world passes away.
His father Almambet
Came riding forth from among the host.
From the side of the noonday sun,
All the forty companions,
With elder Kyrgyl at their head,
Appeared as though slaughter had struck,
Like arrows fiercely loosed,
As though returning to dwell among men,
As though they would drive and devour
All the world.
Renowned among the renowned were those heroes,
Illustrious, fierce-eyed champions,
Red-speared lions
Who had subdued the whole world
With their might.
While the lion Manas lived,
The forty companions were highly honored;
“Companion” was a formidable word—
Not forty companions, but forty comrades.
Each of the forty followed a different path,
All forty had broad white blazes,
Each of the forty had a different nature,
Each grim champion could shatter an age.
Words lose worth when said too often;
Among the forty companions,
There were all kinds, lacking none:
Some were so fierce that water could not penetrate them,
And there were heroic companions
Of gentle nature and open countenance.
There were also harsh companions,
Hot-tempered and abrupt.
There were heroic companions
Who never retreated from battle,
Never shrank a hair’s breadth from death,
Who turned their chargers’ heads
And stood beneath the banner.
There were clumsy companions
Who could not speak and had no words,
Who had chests but no substance,
Black heads and forked legs,
Human only in name,
